Where the north side actually starts: Loop 410 to 1604, and why Castle Hills, Shavano Park and Stone Oak feel like three different cities
Inside 1604 for a Medical Center job: Oak Hills, Churchill Estates and Deerfield. older homes, mature trees, and the shortest drive to Floyd Curl and Wurzbach

script.title: Best North San Antonio Neighborhoods for Veterans, Compared
script.hook: If you're a veteran with a hundred percent rating, Texas can knock your property tax bill down to nothing. And I still watch veterans move to the north side of San Antonio and end up paying on something every year they never planned for. Because two of the three areas everybody points you to have a line on the bill that exemption does not touch.
script.promise: By the end of this you'll know how the north side actually splits up, which parts sit closest to Randolph, Fort Sam and the VA hospital, and the one fee to look for before you sign anything past the outer loop.

sections.title: Where the north side actually starts: Loop 410 out to 1604

takes.text: North San Antonio is not one place. It's three, and they sit in rings. Loop 410 is the inner highway loop, that's basically the old edge of the city. 1604 is the outer loop, another eight or nine miles out. Which ring you land in decides your house age, your drive, and what shows up on your tax bill.
takes.direction: Energy up. Use your hands for the two rings, inner and outer.

takes.text: Castle Hills sits just inside Loop 410 on the north side, and it's technically its own little city with its own police department. Most of it went up in the fifties and sixties. Ranch style, low and wide, big lots, oak trees older than the house. Nothing new is being built there. What you buy is what somebody already lived in for forty years.
takes.direction: Play over slow drive-by footage of older ranch homes and big trees.

takes.text: Shavano Park is a couple miles further out, sitting right up against 1604. Also its own small city. Bigger lots, a lot of them close to an acre, and prices to match. It's quiet in a way that surprises people. Deer in the front yard quiet. You're paying for the address and the land, not for a new kitchen.
takes.direction: Quieter delivery. Lot and street B-roll, no interiors.

takes.text: Stone Oak is the third one, and it's the one you've already seen online. It starts just past 1604 and climbs north up the hill from there. Newer than the other two, bigger houses, more of them, shopping on every corner. It's also where the extra fees start showing up on the tax statement.
takes.direction: Wider shots, newer two-story homes, retail corners.

takes.text: Same side of town, three completely different buys. Castle Hills is an old house on a great lot. Shavano is land. Stone Oak is square footage and a newer roof. If you're relocating on orders or buying with a VA loan, the thing that separates these isn't style. It's what the county and the district charge you to live there.
takes.direction: Straight to lens on the last sentence.

sections.boundaryPull: But if your job or your care sits at the Medical Center, one of these rings beats the other two on drive time, and it's not the one with the new houses.

sections.title: Inside 1604 for a Medical Center or VA hospital job

takes.text: The Medical Center is a cluster of hospitals on the northwest side, inside Loop 410. Floyd Curl is the street most of them sit on. Wurzbach is the road that crosses it. And the Audie Murphy VA hospital is right there in the middle of all of it. If you're getting care there regularly, this section is your section.
takes.direction: Slower on the street names. Let them land.

takes.text: Oak Hills sits just south and west of that hospital cluster. It's about as close as you can live without being in a parking lot. Houses from the sixties and seventies, mostly one story, real grown trees. The drive over to Floyd Curl is short on a normal morning. Some days it's five minutes.
takes.direction: Drive-by B-roll, hospital towers in the background if you have it.

takes.text: Churchill Estates is a little further north, still inside 1604, off Northwest Military Highway, which is the road that runs up toward Castle Hills. Bigger two stories, seventies and eighties builds, and a lot of them have been redone inside. Sidewalks, mature trees, and you're still close to Wurzbach.
takes.direction: Neighborhood entrance and tree-lined street shots.

takes.text: Deerfield is the newest of the three inside that ring. Mostly eighties and nineties, sitting up near 1604 off Lockhill Selma, one of the north-south roads inside the loop. Bigger floor plans than Oak Hills, tile roofs on some streets, straight shot down to the hospitals. It's what people pick when they want space but don't want the highway drive.
takes.direction: Wider street shots, show the size difference.

keywords: aerial suburban cul de sac homes

takes.text: Here's the actual trade inside the loop. These homes are older, so you're inspecting foundations, cast iron drain lines, thirty year old ductwork. Budget for that. But you're inside established city limits, where the infrastructure got built decades ago. No new development fee bolted onto your tax statement. That difference is bigger than most people expect.
takes.direction: Flat, matter of fact. This is the setup for the whole video.

spec.title: What the inspection is really for
spec.footnote: Budget for it going in, not after.

sections.boundaryPull: Push past 1604 on 281 and you get a bigger, newer house for the same money, as long as you've actually driven that highway at seven in the morning. Almost nobody does that before they sign.

sections.title: Past 1604 on 281: Stone Oak, Encino Park and Timberwood Park

takes.text: US 281 is the highway that runs straight north out of downtown, past the airport, and up through all the newer neighborhoods. It's the spine of this whole side of town. And between the outer loop and the county line, it is the single biggest reason people either love where they live or regret it.
takes.direction: On camera, ideally near a highway overpass if you can film it.

takes.text: Stone Oak is the big one. It starts just north of 1604 and climbs up the hill from there. Two story homes, mostly two thousands and newer, gated pockets, grocery stores and urgent cares everywhere. If you want a house that already looks like the photos you've been saving at eleven at night, this is that area.
takes.direction: Newer construction B-roll, gated entrances, retail.

keywords: aerial suburban neighborhood texas hill country

takes.text: Encino Park is smaller and quieter, just off 281 near Bulverde Road, which runs parallel to the highway. Late eighties and nineties, so the trees are grown in and the lots are a decent size. It flies under the radar because it doesn't have a giant entrance sign and eleven villages. People who buy there tend to stay a long time.
takes.direction: Slow, warm read. Quiet street footage.

takes.text: Timberwood Park is further north, past Stone Oak, and it's a different animal. Half acre and acre lots. Some homes on well water and septic. It's unincorporated Bexar County, which means no city property tax line on your bill. That's real money every year. It also means county sheriff instead of city police, and a longer drive to everything.
takes.direction: Big lot and open land B-roll.

keywords: texas hill country homes acreage aerial

takes.text: Drive 281 before you sign. Not on a Saturday afternoon. On a Tuesday, at seven fifteen in the morning, from the actual street you're looking at, to the actual gate or building you report to. That drive is one thing at noon and it is a completely different thing at seven. I've had people change neighborhoods entirely after doing it once.
takes.direction: Say this one slower. It's the most useful sentence in the section.

spec.label: drive the 281 commute before you sign

takes.text: The 281 corridor gets you more house. That part is true. Newer, bigger, better layout for the money. The question is what the drive costs you five days a week for the next three years, and whether the extra line on the tax bill cancels out what you saved on the price.
takes.direction: Straight to lens, calm.

sections.boundaryPull: But if you're reporting to Randolph or Fort Sam, none of this applies, because you're driving the wrong direction entirely, and the northeast side has its own thing nobody warns you about.

sections.title: Northeast for Randolph, Fort Sam Houston and BAMC

takes.text: Three places drive this whole side of town. Randolph is the Air Force base on the northeast side. Fort Sam Houston is the Army post just northeast of downtown. And BAMC, Brooke Army Medical Center, is the big military hospital sitting on Fort Sam. If any of those three is on your orders, stop scrolling 281 listings.
takes.direction: Count them off on your fingers. Energy up.

takes.text: Live Oak and Selma sit right along Interstate 35, the highway that runs northeast out of San Antonio toward Austin. Live Oak is older, eighties and nineties, smaller yards, easier prices. Selma is right next door and newer in spots. Both of them put you close to Randolph and a reasonable drive to Fort Sam outside of rush hour.
takes.direction: Highway and neighborhood B-roll.

takes.text: Universal City is the closest thing to Randolph's front gate. The town grew up around the base and it still feels that way. Modest houses, older, priced under most of what you'll see up north. If you want a short drive and a smaller payment, and you don't need brand new construction, that's the value play on this side of the map.
takes.direction: Calm, honest tone. Older ranch home B-roll.

takes.text: Schertz and Cibolo are the next two out, heading up 35 toward New Braunfels. This is where the new construction lives on the northeast side. Bigger homes, more yard, and a much easier drive to Randolph than anybody sitting up on 281 gets. They've grown fast, and that growth is exactly why the school district question matters here.
takes.direction: New construction B-roll, wide streets.

takes.text: Schertz Cibolo Universal City ISD, people call it SCUC, covers most of those three towns, and it's the one relocating families chase. Judson ISD covers a big piece of the Live Oak side and Converse, the town just south of there. Two districts, same highway, ten minutes apart, and the line does not follow the city limits.
takes.direction: Say SCUC as letters, then as the full name once.

spec.title: Same house, different district
spec.footnote: The line moves the price of the exact same house.

takes.text: That district line moves the price of the exact same house. I've seen two homes, same era, same floor plan, a few miles apart, and the one on the SCUC side sells faster and for more. That's not me grading the schools. That's just what buyers do, and you feel it when you go to sell.
takes.direction: Shrug it off, like you're stating a fact you didn't make up.

sections.boundaryPull: And it gets worse up north, because in Stone Oak that district line runs straight through the neighborhood, and the subdivision name will lie to you about which side you're on.

sections.title: The school boundary surprise: Northside, North East and Comal ISD

takes.text: San Antonio has more than a dozen school districts and they do not line up with city limits, neighborhood names, or anything else that would make sense on a map. This one thing costs people money every single week.
takes.direction: Short take. Straight to lens, a little frustrated.

takes.text: Northside ISD is the giant district covering the west and northwest side. North East ISD covers the north and northeast. Both of them own pieces of Stone Oak. Same subdivision, same entrance sign, and a house on one street feeds one high school while a house three streets over feeds a different one, in a different district.
takes.direction: Play over Stone Oak street footage, no signage close-ups.

spec.eyebrow: Both own pieces of Stone Oak
spec.title: One subdivision, two districts

takes.text: Comal ISD is the district that reaches down from New Braunfels, the town up 35 between here and Austin. It comes a lot further south than people expect. It picks up a chunk of Timberwood Park and it reaches into Cibolo Canyons, a large development east of 281 north of Stone Oak. Bexar County address, district headquartered in another county.
takes.direction: Slower on the last sentence, that is the surprising part.

takes.text: Verify by address. Not by subdivision name, not by what the listing says, not by what the sales office told you on a Saturday. Every district has a boundary lookup where you type in the street address and it hands you the exact campus. Do that before you write an offer. Listings get this wrong constantly, and usually nobody's lying, they just copied the last one.
takes.direction: Firm. This is instruction, not commentary.

takes.text: This matters even if your kids are grown, or you don't have kids at all. Resale. The next buyer is going to look it up, and if your house sits on the wrong side of that line for the neighborhood's reputation, you eat the difference when you sell. Especially on a house you might only hold three or four years on orders.
takes.direction: Bring it back to money. Steady pace.

sections.boundaryPull: And there's one more line on a north side tax bill that your veteran exemption does not touch at all. That's the one I care about most.

sections.title: VA buyers: the disabled veteran exemption versus MUD and PID fees

takes.text: Texas gives disabled veterans a homestead exemption on property taxes that scales with your rating. At a hundred percent service connected, you're exempt on your homestead. That is enormous here, because Texas has no state income tax and leans hard on property tax instead. That exemption is one of the best reasons to buy in this state.
takes.direction: Warm, direct. This is the good news, deliver it like it.

takes.text: Here's the part that catches people. The exemption applies to property taxes. It does not apply to a MUD or a PID. A MUD is a municipal utility district. A PID is a public improvement district. Different setups, same idea. A development outside city services borrowed money to put in the water lines and the roads, and the homeowners pay it back.
takes.direction: Slow down on MUD and PID. Spell out the words.

spec.eyebrow: Two things that are not taxes
spec.title: MUD and PID, plainly
spec.footnote: Your exemption does not touch either one.

takes.text: That charge shows up on the same statement, in the same envelope, looking exactly like a tax. It isn't one. It's an assessment. Your exemption wipes out the school line and the county line, and that assessment just sits there, unchanged, year after year, usually for a couple of decades.
takes.direction: Flat and clear. Let the last line hang.

takes.text: You'll find these north and east of 1604, in the newer developments, the ones with the stone entrance and the amenity center. Inside Loop 410, in Oak Hills, Churchill Estates, Deerfield and Castle Hills, you're generally not dealing with it, because the city put that infrastructure in fifty years ago and it's long paid for.
takes.direction: Contrast the two, newer entrance B-roll then older street B-roll.

takes.text: For a hundred percent rated veteran the math flips completely. A newer house north of 1604 with an assessment on it can cost you more every year than an older house inside the loop with a higher tax rate. Because you're exempt from the tax and you are not exempt from the assessment. Same price tag, different cost to own.
takes.direction: Say this one twice as slow as the rest. It is the thesis.

spec.title: What the exemption does not touch
spec.footnote: It is an assessment, not a tax.

takes.text: Where do veterans actually stay put around here. Universal City, Schertz and Cibolo, over and over, because the drive to Randolph is short and it stays short. Live Oak too, on price. The ones I see back on the market in three years are usually 281 buyers who picked the bigger house first and drove the commute second.
takes.direction: Conversational. Like you're telling a friend what you've noticed.

takes.text: None of this makes Stone Oak or Timberwood a bad buy. Plenty of people love it up there and never look back. Just go in knowing which line on that bill is a tax and which one isn't. Only one of them disappears with your exemption.
takes.direction: Even handed. No edge in the voice.

sections.boundaryPull: Get those two numbers on paper for the exact address you're looking at, and this whole decision gets a lot simpler.

softCta.text: If you already know which base or which hospital you're reporting to, drop it in the comments. I'll tell you which of these areas I'd have you look at first. Takes me a minute.
softCta.direction: Casual, thrown away. Do not sell it.

close.text: Here's what I'd do. Send me the address you're looking at, or just the area and your rating, and I'll run the real numbers. Price, taxes, your exemption, and whether there's a MUD or a PID sitting under that house. Then I'll send you your actual monthly payment in writing, before you fall in love with anything. My number is on the screen and down in the description. Text me, or comment the city you're coming from and I'll answer you. Thanks for watching.
close.direction: Look right at the lens the whole time. Slow, no rush on the last two lines.

sections.title: No state income tax: what Texas takes back instead

takes.text: Before any of it. there's a number on your homeowners policy here that isn't a dollar amount. It's a percentage. And it's the reason a spring hailstorm can cost a family more than they saved all year. I'll show you exactly where it hides. Stay with me, it's coming.
takes.direction: Energy up, straight into the lens, no smile yet

takes.text: Start with the good part. Texas has no state income tax. On a hundred thousand dollar salary, that line is just gone. Federal and payroll still take about a quarter, so you're living on something like seventy-five. Compared to California or New York, that feels like a raise for about six months.
takes.direction: Warm, matter of fact

takes.text: Here's what takes it back. Texas sits near the top of the country for property tax rates. Most of Bexar County. that's the county San Antonio sits in. lands somewhere around two percent of what the county says your house is worth. Every year. Forever. That's not a payment you finish.
takes.direction: Slow down on the last two sentences

takes.text: I worked with a couple who moved here from out of state and built their whole budget off the new take-home. They bought at the top of what the lender approved. Year two, the escrow shortage letter shows up, the payment jumps, and now they're skipping the trip home at Christmas to cover it. Nothing broke. The tax bill just did what tax bills do.
takes.direction: Tell it like you're telling a friend, not warning a client

takes.text: Your payment here is four things stacked together. The loan, the property tax, the homeowners insurance, and mortgage insurance if you put less than twenty percent down. Only the loan part is locked. The other three move, and around here two of them mostly move up.
takes.direction: Count them off on your fingers if you're on camera later

spec.title: What your payment is made of

sections.boundaryPull: Which is why the same money buys three completely different lives in Stone Oak, Alamo Ranch and Converse. Let me spend it in all three.

sections.title: Housing: what your money rents vs buys in Stone Oak, Alamo Ranch and Converse

takes.text: Let's actually spend the money. Same budget, three parts of town. And I'm going to tell you what each one feels like to live in, not just what the square footage says on paper.
takes.direction: Conversational, hands moving

takes.text: Stone Oak is the north side, up 281. that's the highway running north out of downtown. past 1604, the outer loop. Built out in the nineties and two thousands. Hills, big oaks, grown-in yards, and Northside ISD schools people move for. You pay for all of that. Your money buys the least house here of the three.
takes.direction: Neighborhood drive footage, keep the pace easy

takes.text: Alamo Ranch is the far west side, out past 1604 along 151, the highway that runs toward Sea World. Newer. Bigger floor plans for the same money. Smaller lots, thinner trees, and traffic that got ahead of the roads. If you want the most square footage per dollar, it's usually out there.
takes.direction: Even tone, no selling

takes.text: Converse sits northeast, out by Randolph. that's the Air Force base on that side of town. Judson ISD, a mix of older homes and brand new ones, and it's the cheapest of the three by a real margin. Rent's lower too. It's also the furthest from the medical center and the downtown jobs.
takes.direction: Slight lift on 'cheapest'

takes.text: A family I worked with rented in Stone Oak for two years, loved it, couldn't buy there. So they bought in Converse. More house, real backyard, and a kid pulled out of his school in February. He barely spoke to them for a month. They're fine now. But if somebody had asked them one question earlier, they'd have moved in June instead.
takes.direction: Softer here, let the February line land

takes.text: Renting here isn't the waste people tell you it is. Rent in Converse or out west is genuinely reasonable. Six months of renting while you learn the map beats six years in the wrong part of town.
takes.direction: Say this one slower, look right at the lens

sections.boundaryPull: But here's what gets people. Two of those three areas can charge you wildly different tax rates on the exact same price, and the price has nothing to do with it.

sections.title: The tax bill: why the rate follows the address, not the price

takes.text: Your tax rate follows your address. Not your price, not your lender, not your credit. The address. Move the same house half a mile and it costs different money to hold every single year.
takes.direction: Firm, this is the thesis of the video

takes.text: The rate is a stack. The school district is the biggest piece by far. Then the county, the city, the hospital district, the community college, flood control. Add them up and that's your rate. Different addresses sit in different stacks, so they add up to different numbers.
takes.direction: Steady, teaching voice

spec.title: Who is on your tax bill

takes.text: Now the newer stuff. A lot of what got built outside 1604 in the last fifteen years sits in a special district that pays back the roads and pipes that went in first. That gets added to your rate. A house in Stone Oak might sit near two percent. A newer one out by Alamo Ranch can run past three. Same price. Very different year.
takes.direction: Punch 'past three'

takes.text: There's a form that protects you and it costs nothing. The homestead exemption. You file it once with the county appraisal district after you own the house and you're living in it. It knocks the school portion of your taxable value way down, and it caps how much that value can climb to ten percent a year.
takes.direction: Practical, like you're giving instructions

items: Own it and live in it
File with the county appraisal district
Caps taxable value at 10% a year
spec.title: Homestead exemption

takes.text: I had a buyer skip that form. New job, busy, figured the title company handled it. Two years later a neighbor mentions it at a block party. Those two years his value climbed with no cap on it at all, so that bigger number became his starting line going forward. His escrow ate the difference twice. It cost him more than everything he'd bought to furnish the place.
takes.direction: Dry, slightly amused, no lecture

sections.boundaryPull: That percentage on your insurance policy I promised you at the start. that's next. It's the one line newcomers never budget for.

sections.title: Insurance, utilities and hail season

takes.text: Here it is. That's the line I told you about at the start. Open a Texas homeowners policy and find the wind and hail deductible. It's not five hundred bucks. It's a percentage of what your house is insured for.
takes.direction: Hold up a phone or a paper if you have one, energy up

takes.text: One or two percent of your dwelling coverage. On most houses here that's thousands out of your pocket before the company pays anything. And the rest of the policy might still carry a flat deductible, so people read that number, feel fine, and never scroll down to the hail line.
takes.direction: Slow on the numbers

takes.text: A family out west took the cheapest quote their agent sent over the week of closing. Spring storm rolls through, and spring storms here throw hail. Roof's finished. Their deductible was more than they'd saved all year, so they lived under a beat-up roof for two summers and argued about it the whole time.
takes.direction: Let the last line sit for a beat

takes.text: The summer bill. CPS Energy is the city-owned utility here, and July through September is the stretch that surprises people. High ceilings, west-facing glass, an older house inside 410. that's the inner loop. those all show up on the bill. Ask the seller for twelve months of usage. Most of them hand it right over.
takes.direction: Practical tip energy

takes.text: Before you write an offer, ask how old the roof is. A roof past about fifteen years can change your premium here, or land you a policy that only pays what that old roof was worth, not what a new one costs. That's a question for before you're under contract, not after.
takes.direction: Direct, useful, no fluff

items: Replacement cost or actual cash value?
What is the wind and hail deductible?
spec.title: Ask before you offer

sections.boundaryPull: Housing's handled. Now the thing that quietly takes the rest of your money here. and it isn't tolls.

sections.title: Cars, tolls and the 281 and 1604 commute

takes.text: San Antonio doesn't really have a toll network. Austin does. you can spend real money every month just getting to work up there. Down here you pay in something else. Time, and two cars.
takes.direction: Relaxed, this is the breather section

takes.text: There's no commuter train, and the bus isn't built for a suburb-to-office run. So it's two cars for most households. Two payments, two insurance policies, two sets of tires, and gas for a city that spreads out thirty miles corner to corner. That's a real line item and people leave it out of the budget.
takes.direction: Plain, no drama

takes.text: Here's the geography. Downtown sits in the middle. 410 is the inner loop, 1604 is the outer loop, and 281 runs straight north from downtown up through Stone Oak. Almost every north side commute funnels through the spot where 281 and 1604 cross. At five o'clock, that interchange is the whole conversation.
takes.direction: Map voice, clear and slow

takes.text: A dad I worked with bought north of 1604 for the schools. He works at the medical center, that's the cluster of hospitals on the northwest side. On paper it's a twenty-something minute drive. In real life he was missing the first half of every practice. They sold inside a year, moved closer in, took a smaller house, and he says it's the best trade he's ever made.
takes.direction: This one is personal to you, mean it

takes.text: Drive it. Not on a Saturday. Drive from the house to the job at seven fifteen on a Tuesday, then drive it home at five thirty. Twenty-five minutes each way and you're fine. Fifty, and that's five hours a week you never get back. No amount of extra square footage covers that.
takes.direction: Firm, almost an order

sections.boundaryPull: So who actually lives well here on a hundred grand? There's a clean line, and I've watched people land on both sides of it.

sections.title: Who lives comfortably on 100k in San Antonio, and who doesn't

takes.text: A hundred thousand dollars in San Antonio is a comfortable living. It is not an unlimited one. And the difference between those two is almost never the salary. It's the tax rate and the insurance quote on the house you picked.
takes.direction: Look right at the lens, this is the payoff

takes.text: An airman I worked with over by Randolph bought in that corridor, and he bought to his housing allowance instead of to his approval letter. Loan, taxes, insurance, all of it inside the allowance. So his wife's paycheck became the trips, the truck, the savings. Same income as the next guy on base. Completely different life.
takes.direction: Warm, admiring

takes.text: Another buyer, single income, right at that hundred thousand, bought the biggest house the lender would allow. Newer neighborhood outside 1604, special district on the tax bill. Escrow climbed twice in three years. He sold, and that spring there were nine houses just like his on the market. He didn't lose money. He just didn't make any, and he was tired the whole time he owned it.
takes.direction: Flat delivery, let it be sobering

takes.text: When you've got two houses at the same price, pull the tax rate on both and get a real insurance quote on both before you fall in love with either one. That gap is the difference between a vacation every year and a house that owns you.
takes.direction: Steady, this is the takeaway

takes.text: Who this city is easiest on. Two incomes, even modest ones. Anybody carrying pay earned in a more expensive metro. Military families with an allowance that covers the payment. And folks over sixty-five, because Texas freezes the school portion of the bill once you hit that age and file for it.
takes.direction: Count them off, keep it brisk

items: Remote pay from a costlier metro
spec.title: Who it is easiest on

takes.text: Who it's hardest on: one income at a hundred, a long commute, and a house at the very top of the approval. That's not a San Antonio problem. That's a math problem, and you can fix it before you sign anything.
takes.direction: Land it, then hold still for a second

sections.boundaryPull: There's one number I'm not allowed to put in a YouTube video, and it's the number you actually want. Here's how you get it.

softCta.text: Quick thing while you're here. Drop the neighborhood or the base you're looking at in the comments. Just the name. I'll reply with what the tax rate over there actually runs and whether there's a special district sitting on top of it. I read every one of them.
softCta.direction: Casual, half smile, keep it short

close.text: If you want your real number. loan, taxes, insurance, all of it together. text me at the number on the screen. Send me a price and the part of town you're looking at and I'll build the whole thing out and text it back to you. That's me, not an assistant. If texting isn't your thing, comment your budget and which city, San Antonio or Austin, and I'll answer you right there in the thread. Either way you get a real number instead of a guess.
close.direction: Straight to the lens, ask once, then stop talking
